ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic апостольскъ (apostolĭskŭ). By surface analysis, апо́стол (apóstol) + -ский (-skij).
Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ваꙗти (vajati), from Proto-Slavic *vajati, possibly related to Old Church Slavonic вити (viti), Russian вить (vitʹ).

Borrowed from Polish wrocławski. By surface analysis, Вро́цлав (Vróclav) + -ский (-skij).

x: У Фо́геля сиде́ли две гуверна́нтки, на столе́ стоя́ли таре́лки с изю́мом, гре́цкими и минда́льными оре́хами.

ety.text: Pseudo-Gallicism; from диве́рсия (divérsija, “subversion”) + -ант (-ant, agent suffix), with the first element borrowed ultimately from Latin dīversiōnem, via one or several western intermediaries (cf. Polish dywersja, French diversion), and with the second element borrowed from French -ant. No such word as *diversant exists in French.

x: —[...]бы́ло бы о́чень любопы́тно узна́ть, и без промедле́ния, — ско́лько ещё свобо́дный мир бу́дет мири́ться с э́тим тёмным души́телем свобо́ды, де́лая вид, что не замеча́ет неви́нных слёз и брызг кро́ви, летя́щих пря́мо в на́шу о́птику![...]

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic зьданиѥ (zĭdanije). By surface analysis, здать (zdatʹ) + -ание (-anije).

ety.text: Borrowed from French croupier. Omitting several steps, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz + the suffix derived from Latin -ārius. Doublet of гру́ппа (grúppa) and круп (krup).

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣ́мьць (ně́mĭcĭ), from Proto-Slavic *němьcь (“foreigner, German”), from *němъ (“mute”) (whence Russian немо́й (nemój)). Compare typologically Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros), whence ва́рвар (várvar).

ety.text: From a rethought word structure под- (pod-) + -слепова́тый (-slepovátyj), where под- (pod-) is loosely attached. Further from a forgotten подслéпый- (podslépyj-) + -ова́тый (-ovátyj). According to the restriction on the compatibility of morphemes within a word form: the dominant basic component cannot be combined with the dominant suffix, which requires stress to be placed to the right of the basic component.

x: Для обжа́ривания помидо́ры уложи́ть разре́зом вверх на сковороду́, разогре́тую с ма́слом.

ety.text: First used during the Maidan movement in Kiev in 2013. Named after an active mob member called Titushko, Russian: Титу́шко (Titúško), Ukrainian: Тіту́шко (Titúško).

s.g: to variegate, to diversify, to vary

ety.text: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *čùti, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”), whence English show and caution, as well as German schauen (“to look”), thereby English anschauung and weltanschauung (“sense of the world, worldview”).
(minion): The most common Russian card deck has 36 cards, where the six is the first in the suit, whence the sense.
